prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Children from a polygamist sect who one mother says are "hurting very badly" in state custody are likely to be returned to their parents, a CNN legal analyst says. FLDS member Margaret Jessop says her children "feel betrayed by adults." A Texas appeals court ruled Thursday that the state had no right to remove hundreds of children from the Fundamentalist Church of Latter-Day Saints' ranch in Eldorado on April 3, based on the suspicion that a few were being sexually abused. A sect mother who has four children in state custody said the matter has not been fully resolved because an appeal to the Texas Supreme Court is possible. "I'm very grateful, but I'd like to see the children in my arms before I rejoice greatly," Margaret Jessop said on CNN's "Larry King Live."  Watch Jessop react to the ruling » . But a permanent reunion of families is likely, said Jeffrey Toobin, CNN senior legal analyst. "Based on this ruling I think it's clear that if it stands, all these kids are going back with their mothers," Toobin said on CNN's "Anderson Cooper 360°." Jessop and other FLDS parents said they had been permitted visits with their children in foster care. Zavenda Young said two of her children were sent to Waco, Texas, and two to Hockley, 148 miles away. "They're in Boys and Girls Country in Hockley. And it's just a -- it's an institution," she told host Larry King. Their father, Edson Jessop, said the experience has been rough on the children. "You can see it's a lot of stress on them," he said. "Every time we leave, they go through that trauma again. It's enough to rip your heart out." "They feel betrayed by adults, and they're hurting very badly," Margaret Jessop added. The Texas Child Protective Services Department's Web site says the agency has been "coordinating with many professional service and government agencies to ensure the safety, health and comfort of the children and women in Eldorado." A statement from the agency Thursday said it's working out a response to the court ruling. "Child Protective Services has one duty -- to protect children," the statement said. "When we see evidence that children have been sexually abused and remain at risk of further abuse, we will act. ... We will work with the office of the attorney general to determine the state's next step in this case."

A Texas appeals court ruled that state officials lacked sufficient evidence to justify the sweeping removal of hundreds of children from the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints ranch near Eldorado.

The children were taken into state custody after authorities raided the Yearning for Zion Ranch amid allegations that underage girls were being forced into spiritual marriages with older men and subjected to sexual abuse. Child-welfare officials argued that the community’s beliefs and practices placed all children at risk, even when there was no specific evidence that an individual child had been abused.

Parents challenged the removals, saying the state had treated the ranch’s entire population as a single household rather than evaluating each family and child separately. They also described children becoming frightened, confused and emotionally distressed after being separated from their parents and placed in foster-care facilities around Texas.

The appeals court concluded that the state had not shown an immediate danger to every child sufficient to warrant emergency removal. In particular, it said officials had failed to present evidence that boys and girls who had not reached puberty faced an imminent risk of abuse. Concerns about the FLDS community’s general belief system, the court found, could not substitute for proof involving individual children or families.

The ruling did not resolve the underlying allegations of abuse or prevent Texas from investigating particular cases. Nor did it bar the state from seeking protective orders when evidence showed that a specific child was in danger. Instead, the decision held that authorities could not remove all the children simply because some members of the community were suspected of misconduct.

If the ruling remained in effect, the state would be required to return the affected children to their families, potentially under court-ordered conditions and continued monitoring. Texas officials could ask the state Supreme Court to overturn or delay the decision, leaving the timing of any reunifications uncertain.

For the FLDS parents, however, the appellate decision represented a major victory. It shifted the legal focus away from broad suspicions about the ranch and toward the state’s obligation to demonstrate an immediate, individualized threat before separating children from their families.

### CNN Coverage of Children in the FLDS Community

In 2008, CNN and other major news organizations closely followed events surrounding the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, commonly known as the FLDS. The religious group, which is not affiliated with the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, attracted national attention after Texas authorities removed hundreds of children from the Yearning for Zion Ranch near Eldorado.

Officials said they were responding to concerns about child abuse and underage marriage. FLDS families disputed many of the allegations and argued that the removal violated their parental and religious rights. CNN reported on the legal proceedings, interviewed family members and examined the difficult questions facing child-welfare authorities.

The case generated a national debate about how governments should protect children while respecting religious freedom and due process. The Texas Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the state had not provided sufficient evidence to justify placing all the children in protective custody, and many were returned to their families. Nevertheless, investigations into specific allegations continued.

CNN’s coverage brought public attention to the experiences of children in isolated religious communities. It also illustrated the importance of careful, evidence-based reporting when stories involve minors, family separation, faith and alleged abuse.

**Texas appeals court: State improperly removed children from FLDS ranch**

**AUSTIN, Texas (CNN)** — A Texas appeals court ruled Thursday that state officials improperly removed hundreds of children from a polygamist sect’s ranch, finding that child-welfare authorities failed to show the children faced an immediate danger that justified placing them in state custody.

The 3rd Court of Appeals in Austin said the trial court abused its discretion when it authorized the removal of children from the Yearning for Zion Ranch near Eldorado, operated by members of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints.

More than 400 children were taken from the ranch in April after authorities received a report alleging abuse of a teenage girl. Investigators later said they believed the sect’s practice of arranging marriages involving underage girls created a pervasive risk of sexual abuse.

But the appellate court said the state had not presented sufficient evidence that every child removed from the ranch was in immediate danger or that less drastic measures could not have protected them. The ruling directed the lower court to vacate its temporary-custody orders.

Margaret and Edson Jessop, FLDS parents whose children were among those taken, welcomed the decision and said they wanted their family reunited. The couple maintained that their children had not been abused and argued that the state treated all families at the ranch as though they faced the same circumstances.

Child Protective Services spokeswoman Zavenda Young said the agency was disappointed by the decision and was reviewing its legal options. CPS continued to argue that conditions at the ranch placed children—particularly adolescent girls—at risk.

CNN senior legal analyst Jeffrey Toobin described the ruling as a major setback for Texas. He said the decision reflected a basic legal problem with the state’s case: Officials had acted against the ranch’s children as a group without establishing an immediate threat to each individual child.

The ruling did not end the state’s child-abuse investigations or prevent CPS from pursuing cases involving specific families. It did, however, reject the broad legal basis used for the mass removal and opened the way for parents to seek the return of their children.

The FLDS church, a breakaway Mormon sect, practices polygamy. The mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints renounced plural marriage more than a century ago and is not affiliated with the FLDS.

**AUSTIN, Texas —** Hundreds of children taken from a polygamist sect’s West Texas ranch could soon be reunited with their parents after the Texas Supreme Court ruled that state officials had not justified removing the entire group from their homes.

The ruling left intact an appeals court decision finding that the state failed to show that all of the children at the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints’ Yearning for Zion Ranch faced an immediate risk of abuse. More than 400 children were placed in foster care following an April raid on the ranch near Eldorado.

In interviews on CNN’s **“Larry King Live”** and **“Anderson Cooper 360°,”** parents, attorneys and child-welfare advocates described families awaiting detailed reunification orders while the state continued investigating allegations of underage marriage and sexual abuse.

Attorneys for FLDS families said the ruling vindicated their argument that Texas authorities treated the ranch’s children as a single group instead of presenting evidence about danger to each child. They stressed that the decision did not end the broader child-protection cases or prevent officials from acting when evidence exists against particular parents.

Texas child-welfare officials maintained that investigators had encountered a culture in which girls could be prepared for spiritual marriages at young ages. The courts, however, concluded that those concerns were not enough to support the emergency removal of every child, including boys and very young children, without individualized proof of imminent danger.

The children were expected to remain under court supervision as district-court officials developed terms for their return. Possible conditions included allowing state investigators access to the children, notifying authorities of changes in residence and complying with additional protective orders.

The legal battle began after authorities received calls alleging abuse at the ranch. Questions later emerged about the identity and credibility of the caller, but officials said evidence gathered during the raid prompted continuing investigations.

The FLDS, a breakaway Mormon sect that practices polygamy, is not affiliated with the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which renounced plural marriage more than a century ago.

The ruling represents a major setback for Texas authorities, but it does not resolve allegations involving individual families. Those cases may continue separately even as most of the children return to their parents.

# Hundreds of children taken from polygamist sect’s ranch could soon return home

**AUSTIN, Texas (CNN)** — Hundreds of children removed from a polygamist sect’s West Texas ranch may soon be reunited with their families after the state’s highest court ruled that child welfare officials did not present sufficient evidence to justify taking every child into state custody.

The Texas Supreme Court declined to overturn an appellate court decision finding that the mass removal of children from the Yearning for Zion Ranch was improper. The ruling could clear the way for more than 400 children to return to their parents, provided families comply with conditions imposed by a lower court.

Texas Child Protective Services said it would work to reunite the families but continued to defend the April raid, arguing that investigators encountered a community in which underage girls were at risk of being drawn into sexual relationships with older men.

State officials said the agency faced an unusual situation involving an isolated religious community, complicated family relationships and what investigators described as a culture that normalized marriages involving girls younger than the legal age of consent.

The children were taken from the ranch near Eldorado, about 45 miles south of San Angelo, after authorities received a call alleging that a teenage girl was being abused. Questions later emerged about whether the caller existed, but CPS said evidence gathered during the investigation raised concerns extending beyond the original report.

Attorneys for the families argued that the state treated the entire ranch as a single household and failed to show that each child faced an immediate threat. They also said many of the children — including infants and young boys — had no connection to the alleged abuse.

The courts agreed that Texas law required more individualized evidence before children could be removed from their parents.

The Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, or FLDS, broke from the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints more than a century ago. The mainstream Mormon church renounced polygamy in 1890 and has no affiliation with the FLDS.

The return of the children does not end the state’s investigation. CPS may continue monitoring families and pursuing individual cases where it believes a child is in danger. Parents could also be required to cooperate with home visits, disclose their children’s whereabouts and follow restrictions intended to protect minors while the cases proceed.

CPS officials said the court’s ruling addressed whether the state met the legal standard for emergency removal, not whether abuse had occurred at the ranch. They maintained that the agency acted to protect children based on the information available at the time.

Family members, meanwhile, said they were eager for reunification after weeks of separation and court hearings. Lawyers were expected to work with the trial court on arrangements for releasing the children, with some reunions possible within days.
